question: A 55-year-old man presents for physical and preventive health screening, specifically for prostate cancer. He has not been to the doctor in a long time. Past medical history is significant for hypertension that is well-managed. Current medication is hydrochlorothiazide. He has one uncle who died of prostate cancer. He drinks one or two alcoholic drinks on the weekends and does not smoke. Today his temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F), blood pressure is 125/75 mm Hg, pulse is 82/min, respiratory rate is 15/min, and oxygen saturation is 99% on room air. There are no significant findings on physical examination. Which of the following would be the most appropriate recommendation for prostate cancer screening in this patient?

options.opa: No screening indicated at this time
options.ope: Contrast CT of the abdomen and pelvis

analysis: For a 55-year-old man with a family history of prostate cancer (one uncle), the recommendation for prostate cancer screening would typically include discussing the potential benefits and risks of screening with the patient and considering a serum PSA (Prostate-Specific Antigen) test. The digital rectal examination (DRE) is less commonly used alone for screening due to its lower sensitivity compared to PSA testing. Transrectal ultrasound (TRUS) and contrast CT of the abdomen and pelvis are not standard initial screening tools for prostate cancer. They are more often used in diagnostic evaluation after abnormal screening results. Therefore, the most appropriate initial screening test in this scenario, considering the patient's age and family history, would be a serum PSA level.
